overview.text: Mount Vesuvius (Vesuvio) is a composite volcano on the Bay of Naples in southern Italy. Its distinctive form pairs a younger cone with the caldera rim of the older Monte Somma volcano. In 79 CE, an explosive eruption sent ash, pumice, and hot pyroclastic currents across the region, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum. The eruption style is called “Plinian” after Pliny the Younger, who described the event. Vesuvius erupted again in later centuries, most recently in 1944. Although it has not erupted since, it remains an active volcano monitored by Italian authorities. Its history matters both for the Roman towns preserved beneath volcanic deposits and for the continuing hazard near Naples.

key_facts.text: Vesuvius rises beside the Bay of Naples in southern Italy.
The Somma-Vesuvius complex has a younger Vesuvius cone inside the caldera of older Monte Somma.
The 79 CE eruption buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in volcanic material, including ash, pumice, and pyroclastic deposits.
The last eruption was in 1944; the volcano is monitored by Italy’s Vesuvius Observatory.
Pliny the Younger’s description of the 79 CE eruption gave the Plinian eruption style its name.
